lessons.title: What is word stress?
lessons.explain: Every English word of two or more syllables has one strong syllable. The strong one is longer, louder and clearer.
points: Stressed syllable: longer, louder, clear vowel.
Unstressed syllable: short and often a schwa /ə/.
Only one primary stress per word.

items.note: Two syllables, stress on the first.

lessons.title: Stress that changes the word
lessons.explain: Some words change meaning or word class when the stress moves. Say both versions and feel the difference.
points: Nouns often stress the first syllable.
Verbs often stress the second syllable.

items.note: I want to record my voice.
There is an increase in price.

lessons.title: Word families and secondary stress
lessons.explain: When you add an ending, the stress often moves. Longer words also have a weaker secondary beat.
points: Primary stress: the strongest beat.
Secondary stress: a smaller beat, usually earlier in the word.

lessons.title: More noun/verb stress pairs
lessons.explain: This noun/verb pattern is very common — dozens of English words work this way.
points: Noun = stress first syllable.
Verb = stress second syllable.

lessons.title: Even more noun/verb pairs
lessons.explain: Keep practising this pattern until switching the stress feels automatic.
points: Listen for the vowel quality change too, not just loudness.

lessons.title: Two-syllable nouns: first-syllable stress
lessons.explain: Most two-syllable English nouns stress the first syllable.
points: This is the default pattern for nouns — assume first syllable unless you learn otherwise.

lessons.title: Two-syllable verbs: second-syllable stress
lessons.explain: Most two-syllable English verbs stress the second syllable — the opposite of nouns.
points: This is the default pattern for verbs.

lessons.title: -tion and -sion always take the stress before them
lessons.explain: Words ending in -tion or -sion always stress the syllable right before the ending.
points: -tion / -sion → stress moves to the syllable just before it.

items.note: Exception pattern — check a dictionary if unsure.

lessons.title: -ic and -ical always take the stress before them
lessons.explain: Words ending in -ic or -ical stress the syllable right before the ending, just like -tion.
points: -ic / -ical → stress the syllable before the ending.

lessons.title: -ity and -ety always take the stress before them
lessons.explain: Another reliable rule: -ity and -ety pull the stress onto the syllable right before them.
points: -ity / -ety → stress the syllable before the ending.

lessons.title: Prefixes usually don't take the stress
lessons.explain: Adding un-, re-, dis- or non- to a word doesn't move the stress — the prefix stays weak.
points: un- / re- / dis- / non- are almost never stressed.

items.note: A common exception — 'nonsense' stresses the first syllable.

lessons.title: Compound nouns: stress the first word
lessons.explain: When two words combine into one noun, the first word usually carries the stress.
points: Compound NOUN → stress word 1.
Compare with phrasal adjectives, which stress word 2 (see next lesson).

lessons.title: Adjective + noun phrases: stress the second word
lessons.explain: Compare this to the last lesson: when it's really an adjective describing a noun (two separate words, two meanings), the stress moves to the noun.
points: black BIRD = a bird that is black (any bird).
BLACKbird = one specific kind of bird.

items.note: Any bird that happens to be black.
Compare: WHITEhouse (compound) doesn't exist — this stays two words.
A dog that is hot (not the food, HOT dog).

lessons.title: Numbers: -teen vs -ty
lessons.explain: Thirteen and thirty are often confused. The stress placement is the main difference.
points: -TEEN numbers: stress the second syllable.
-ty numbers: stress the first syllable.

items.note: Exaggerate the contrast so listeners can tell them apart.

lessons.title: Job titles and professions
lessons.explain: Job-title vocabulary you'll use constantly in small talk and interviews.
points: Most end in -er/-or/-ist and stress the syllable before that ending.

items.note: Exception — stress falls on the last syllable.

lessons.title: Technology vocabulary
lessons.explain: Common tech words — useful for work meetings and everyday conversation about phones and computers.

items.note: Noun/verb — stress stays on the first syllable in both.

lessons.title: Business and office vocabulary
lessons.explain: Words you'll say in every meeting — get the stress right and you'll sound confident at work.

lessons.title: Travel and tourism vocabulary
lessons.explain: Practise these before your next trip — mispronouncing 'hotel' or 'airport' is a common stumbling block.

lessons.title: Food and cooking vocabulary
lessons.explain: Everyday food words — great for restaurant conversations.

lessons.title: Family and relationship words
lessons.explain: Talking about family is one of the first things learners need — stress these correctly from the start.

lessons.title: Emotion words
lessons.explain: Describing feelings accurately needs the right stress, or listeners may mishear the word entirely.

lessons.title: Countries and nationalities
lessons.explain: Country and nationality names often have unexpected stress for learners.

lessons.title: -ous and -eous adjectives
lessons.explain: Adjectives ending in -ous almost always stress the syllable right before the ending.
points: -ous → stress the syllable before it.

lessons.title: -ial and -ual adjectives
lessons.explain: Like -ous, endings -ial and -ual usually pull stress onto the syllable right before them.

lessons.title: -ate: noun/adjective vs verb
lessons.explain: Words ending in -ate can be a noun/adjective (shorter vowel, earlier stress) or a verb (long 'ate' /eɪt/, later stress).
points: Noun/adjective -ate: shorter, earlier stress.
Verb -ate: full /eɪt/ sound, often later stress.

items.note: Rarely used as a verb — 'certify' is more common.

lessons.title: Acronyms and abbreviations
lessons.explain: When you spell out an abbreviation letter by letter, the LAST letter usually gets the strongest stress.
points: Spelling out letters: last letter is strongest.

lessons.title: Days, months and time words
lessons.explain: Time vocabulary is used in every conversation, so get the stress automatic early.

lessons.title: Loanwords from French
lessons.explain: English borrowed many French words and often keeps the final-syllable stress they had in French.
points: French loanwords often stress the LAST syllable — the opposite of typical English nouns.

items.note: British English often says GAR-age instead.

lessons.title: Compound adjectives with hyphens
lessons.explain: Hyphenated adjectives before a noun usually stress the second part more when spoken alone, but level out when placed before the noun they describe.

lessons.title: Three-syllable words: pattern practice
lessons.explain: Three-syllable words often stress the first syllable, but not always — always double-check unfamiliar words.

items.note: Exception — stress on the middle syllable.
Exception — stress on the middle syllable.

lessons.title: Adjective/noun pairs with the -al ending
lessons.explain: Words ending in -al often keep the stress in the same place as their root word.

items.note: Stress does shift here — an exception to watch for.

lessons.title: Sports and hobbies vocabulary
lessons.explain: Talking about hobbies is classic small-talk material — get comfortable with this vocabulary.

lessons.title: Weather vocabulary
lessons.explain: Weather talk is universal small talk — make sure the stress is automatic.

lessons.title: Health and medical vocabulary
lessons.explain: Useful, sometimes urgent vocabulary — worth practising until it's automatic.

lessons.title: Education vocabulary
lessons.explain: School and study vocabulary — common in IELTS Speaking Part 1 too.

lessons.title: Finance and money vocabulary
lessons.explain: Money vocabulary shows up constantly — from shopping to salary negotiations.

lessons.title: Verb + noun stress-shift practice
lessons.explain: Final round of the noun/verb stress-shift pattern — by now it should start to feel automatic.

items.note: British English often stresses the second syllable for both.

lessons.title: Adjective endings: -able and -ible
lessons.explain: -able and -ible usually don't change the stress of the root word.

lessons.title: Longer academic words
lessons.explain: Academic English uses long, Latin-based words — apply the -tion/-ity/-ic rules you've already learned.

lessons.title: Everyday greetings and expressions
lessons.explain: You'll say these words every single day — stress them naturally from day one.

lessons.title: City and place-name stress
lessons.explain: Place names sometimes break the usual rules — worth practising the common ones by heart.

items.note: Often BANG-kok in casual American speech too.

lessons.title: Verbs ending in -ize / -ise
lessons.explain: Verbs ending in -ize (US) or -ise (UK) keep the stress on the syllable before the ending.

lessons.title: Emphatic stress on longer descriptive adjectives
lessons.explain: Descriptive adjectives you'll use to make small talk more vivid.

lessons.title: Words that look similar but stress differently
lessons.explain: Spelling doesn't always predict stress — these near-twins trip up even advanced learners.

lessons.title: Practice set: mixed review
lessons.explain: A final mixed set pulling together nouns, verbs, suffix rules and compounds — say each one before checking the pattern.

lessons.title: Phrasal verb vs compound noun
lessons.explain: A phrasal verb stresses the particle; the noun made from it stresses the first part instead.
points: Verb: break DOWN, print OUT.
Noun: a BREAKdown, a PRINTout.

lessons.title: Big numbers and money amounts
lessons.explain: Hundred, thousand and million are never stressed themselves — the number just before them carries the beat.

lessons.title: Common idioms and fixed expressions
lessons.explain: Idioms have their own fixed stress pattern learners should memorise as a whole chunk.

lessons.title: Words that lose a syllable in fast speech
lessons.explain: Some common words are almost always said with one fewer syllable than they're spelled with — this changes where the stress lands.

lessons.title: Final mixed review
lessons.explain: One last mixed set — nouns, verbs, compounds and suffix rules together. Say each one before checking the pattern.
